messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorph community,

I'm investigating brain shape variation in mustelids which are thought to be an adaptive radiation. The phylogenetic signal for brain shape indicates a departure from Brownian motion (K=0.48039; p=1e-04).

I've also run PGLS analyses with brain shape as a function of ecological/body size variables. I checked the phylogenetic signal of the residuals, and in nearly every case, K is between 0.5 to 0.6 and  p=1e-04.

A suggested fix was to transform the phylogenetic tree before running further evolutionary analyses. My questions are:
(1) What does it mean to "transform" a tree?
(2) Do you have any advice/resources on how to accomplish this?
(3) Will this approach work with the new updates to Geomorph? Is there a different way to address this issue?

---------------------------------------
Unrelated side question: I keep getting different numbers for the PC loadings when I run a PCA, even though I'm using the exact same data set every time. It started happening after the big updates went through. Anyone know why this is? (e.g., one time the variance explained by PC1 may be 35%, and the next time running the analysis, it's 38%)

Hi there,

Phylogenetic transformations are different transformations of the matrix representations of the phylogeny. Some examples include the lambda transform, kappa, delta, etc. Some details are provided here (https://rdrr.io/rforge/motmot/man/transformPhylo.html), but I encourage you to track down the original papers for a full description of the different methods and what they mean.

Geomorph can do a lambda transform which I think might be what you are looking for. Take a look at the procD.pgls documentation here (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/geomorph.pdf). The vignettes also go over how to optimize the parameter in regression using permutations.

To answer your side question, I think folks might need more info (like the version numbers you are using).

Best,
Bryan

messages.body_plain:
Bryan is correct that the tree scaling parameter, lambda, can be adjusted in procD.pgls.  There is an indirect way to also vary other scaling parameters, with the scaleCov function in RRPP.  This would require understanding how there parameters change a covariance matrix obtained from a tree, and working with the covariance matrix, directly, rather than the tree.  (The procD.pgls function calculates the covariance matrix from the tree, but covariance matrices could be obtained independently, e.g., with ape::vcv.phylo.)

Regarding this question:

> > > Unrelated side question: I keep getting different numbers for the PC loadings when I run a PCA, even though I'm using the exact same data set every time. It started happening after the big updates went through. Anyone know why this is? (e.g., one time the variance explained by PC1 may be 35%, and the next time running the analysis, it's 38%)

You might not be using the exact same data, if obtained from gpagen (and I doubt the RRPP::ordinate or geomorph::gm.prcomp functions have changed in any way to induce drastically different loadings).  Several versions back (maybe the “big updates”), we started using faster algorithms for gpagen with sliding semilandmarks.  This meant more iterations could be run in the same amount of time, so we changed the default for max.iter from a maximum of 5 to 10 iterations (but one could run many more by changing the argument).  If you have semilandmarks and used the default arguments for gpagen, then what you might think are the exact same data are actually different data, if obtained before and after the update.

As a note on this and maybe as a surprise for some, GPA does not produce exact data.  The result depends on the convergence criterion used for this iterative procedure, if one requires convergence, or if not, when to stop the analysis.  These decisions are arbitrary.  Unless users wish to be confronted with an analysis that never ends, the default is to arrest the analysis after 10 iterations.  This is neither a rule of thumb nor a recommendation — we simply need to have something as a default.  With sliding landmarks, there is rarely convergence.  In fact, in some cases one could start to find results that are increasingly bad, as landmarks slide past each other, and variance among configurations is minimized by finding morphological impossibilities.  This is under-appreciated area of research in need of more theoretical development!  However, one could empirically explore for an optimal number of iterations (minimize variance while retaining morphological reasonableness).

If you wish to have exactly the same data, first decide how many GPA iterations are needed, and always use that number for the set of raw landmarks.  If you want to try to make your results look like they used to, try max.iter = 5 and see if that helps.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject_clean: Phylogenetic PCA + use of data that is corrected for phylogenetic signal
messages.body_plain:
Hi Geomorph community,

In my dataset on distal ulnar shape I want to check for a phylogenetic signal and, if present, I want to correct for a phylogenetic signal in the subsequent analyses. I have a few questions/remarks about this as I have no experience using phylogeny in data-analysis (and reading all the different approaches freaks me out a little bit ...).

1) To run a phylogenetic PCA, I have to use the mean shape of the different primate taxa in combination with a phylogenetic tree (which shows the same taxa). I did some research on how to perform this in R, and I came across this description (Almecija, 2015):

"To assess the phylogenetic patterning in the shape space, we mapped a phylogenetic tree onto the shape space defined by the two first axes of a PCA of the covariance
matrix of extant taxa means. Hypothetical ancestral states (internal nodes in the tree) were reconstructed using squared-change parsimony (Maddison, 1991) with a method developed for geometric data in which shape is treated as a single multidimensional
character and weighed by branch length (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). Subsequently, the estimated ancestral node configurations were plotted on the original
shape space, and the branches of the tree were connected to obtain a phylomorphospace (Rohlf, 2002; Sidlauskas, 2008; Monteiro, 2013)."

I have to admit that, since I'm not familiar with using phylogeny in PCA analyses, this is hard for me to follow. According to this description, I cannot simply use a phylogenetic tree in combination with mean shapes, and additional parameters need to be added to get a proper phylogenetic PCA?

2) If there is a phylogenetic signal in the dataset, I want to correct for it because I have to use phylogenetic-corrected data in the subsequent analyses. Is it possible to do this without having to use mean shapes in the subsequent analyses? Because this means losing all the variance, which would then prevent from testing differences between the species themselves ... Most tools seem to assume that, when you want to control for phylogeny, you are testing according to a different grouping variable that is not the species itself (e.g. locomotor groups)?

In the paper mentioned above, this is what is said in the method section:

"The previous steps were necessary to subsequently test for the presence of a phylogenetic signal in hamate shape space by means of a permutation test approach (Laurin, 2004) extended for multivariate analysis of coordinate data (Klingenberg and Gidaszewski, 2010). This technique simulates the null hypothesis of complete absence of phylogenetic structure among hamate shapes in extant anthropoids. The species mean shape configurations were randomly distributed as the TIPS of the phylogeny in 10,000 permutations. For each permutation, tree length (i.e., the sum of the squared Procrustes distances between ancestral and descendant shapes for all branches) was computed. If more than 5% of the resulting tree lengths computed in the permutation test were greater than the one obtained with the original data, the null hypothesis of absence of phylogenetic structure in the data was rejected."
Again, as I'm not familiar with the different terms, I don't really understand. Is the function "phylosig" OK to use to test for a phylogenetic signal? And I also don't see HOW they corrected the data for the phylogenetic signal.

I'm very sorry for my extensive question. I'm quite new in the field, and people saying "It's not that difficult' do not help either ... In general, it would be nice if someone here would be happy to help me (e.g. during a skype call) with these analyses. I have a full R script for my PCA analyses, 2B-PLS analyses, ... but I can really use some guidance on how to properly implement phylogeny into this story. Of course, you can be co-author on the publication (will normally be published in a Mary Marzke special issue of the American Journal of Biological Anthropology).

Thank you very much.

Marie.

Marie,

The descriptions from the papers you cited are correct, but one does not need to do all of those steps by hand. For instance, the function ‘gm.prcomp’ in geomorph will provide ordinations of one’s data, and if you provide the function with a phylogeny, it will allow you to obtain one of 3 ordinations with phylogeny: 1 a phylomorphospace (a PCA with the phylogeny projected into that space), a phylogenetic-PCA (ala Revell 2009), or a PACA plot: phylogenetically aligned components analysis (ala Collyer and Adams 2021). Note that projecting the phylogeny into the PCA is NOT a phylogenetic-PCA (as you stated). It instead is a phylomorphospace. Phylogenetic PCA accounts for the phylogeny during the rotation step.  Give a careful read to Collyer and Adams 2021 who describe all 3 approaches.

For phylogenetic signal, one can evaluate this using the function physignal.  This using Kmult, the multivariate generalization of Blomberg’s kappa (Adams 2014). It is not the same procedure as described in Klingenberg’s paper, which is discussed in my paper.

For PLS, one can account for the phylogeny using phylo.integration; again in geomorph.

Note that one really should read the primary literature and understand what these methods and approaches are doing mathematically. We have several review papers on multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods (Adams and Collyer 2018, 2019) which are available on my web page. They survey many of these and other approaches.

Best,

Dean

Marie,

Yes, phylogenetic comparative methods all require that there is a ‘match’ between the data and the phylogeny. Thus, since there is one tip per species, one requires one data point. That is typically the mean of a sample of specimens for that species. Some other points of corection

PGLS tests for associations between dependent (Y) and independent (X) variables while accounting for phylogeny. It was unclear what you were testing (you need both X and Y variables)

One does not need to do a PCA with residuals of the PGLS, though many papers do this; thinking that they are working with phylogenetically ‘corrected’ data. I do not prefer that term, and prefer to work with pPCA and PACA which includes the data and the phylogeny directly in the ordination.

Dean

Thank you for your reply. I indeed came across your 2021 paper on the different methods and if I understand correctly, what I basically need to do (for both phy-PCA or PACA) is:

- I use phylosignal to test for a phylogenetic signal in the dataset (which can run both the lambda and K on PC scores)

- as a complement to that, I can run a PGLS and test the effect of phylogeny in my sample

- if this is significant, I do a PCA with the residuals of that test and get phylogenetically corrected data to work with

BUT, what confuses me is that when I implement a phylogenetic tree into the function this would mean that I need to work with mean shapes, no? Otherwise the number of datapoints won't match with the number of tips of the tree. And using mean shapes implies losing all variance between the different specimens? Or maybe this does not matter because I can use the residuals in the subsequent PCA analyses and test for significant differences between the different specimens.

And what I understand from your paper is that, because PACA shows variations most associated with phylogenetic signal while in phy-PCA this is most independent of phylogenetic variation, it would be best to use both tests next to each other.

All the best,

Marie

library(geomorph)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Katie,

It is difficult to replicate read.morphologika errors because errors are usually dependent on the files that are in a specific directory on one’s computer.  This function has not been updated in a long time.  I was able to verify the function works with a morphologika file I found online, saved in a fresh directory, and I was able to verify if an alternative .txt file was added to that directory, the function caught that it was not a morpholgika-formatted file.  Note that this is an old function that basically provides a loop to use an internal function, read.one.morphologika, binding each set of landmark data from each file onto a growing matrix, which is converted into an array at the end.  The error you received indicates that one of the files has a different number of landmarks (or landmarks in more or fewer dimensions) than the files that preceded it.  The function could do a better job of indicating with which file the reading of data was arrested, but that would mean the error would still be triggered, even if a better explanation could be offered.

If I were in your shoes, I would create a new empty directory, copy and add one file from the other directory, and make sure the function works after creating a file list with just one file.  Then I would copy the files, one by one, from the other directory and re-run until I determined which file caused the error, so I could investigate what is going on with that particular file.

There are a few possible explanations.  One is that you might have added new files to the directory since the time it worked, or altered some files within (even if not intentional)  Another is that R could have changed something with its scan function that is the workhorse for any read.something function, and certain files might trigger a problem that was not there before the alteration.  This is just a guess — don’t know the history of scan updates.  It is also possible updates to strsplit or grep function in R were made.

Unfortunately, a trial and error approach will be needed to better determine which file or files cause errors.  I hope it is a simple change to the file list on your end, as that would be easy to fix.  This function has not been updated since 2017 so it is likely not a geomorph change that caused your error.  Hopefully it is not an incompatible R update.

Best,
Mike

Although morphologika files, like tps or nts files, as well, contain the values for Cartesian coordinates, and are, therefore, possible data repositories, I feel read.morphologika should be used only once for the express purpose of acquiring data that could be saved in a more reasonable format, including csv files or Rdata objects.  Whether you recover your ability to acquire data from your morphologika files or are happy with the coercion effort, I recommend saving all of the objects you wish to work with again (using the save function) as an Rdata object.  Then your script can simply use the load function to reload the various data, and possibly, saved analyses.  Rdata objects should be more robust with respect to the changes R makes, and won’t care if you mangle text files along the way.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question about the phylogenetic PCA (phyPCA) and phylogenetic aligned component analysis (PaCA). At this point, I'm using both to study shape variation in the ulna of different primate taxa. However, I'm a bit confused on how I can test for significant differences between groups.

In a previous analysis in which I used a regular PCA, I used an ANCOVA to test for differences between the different primate species (e.g. cimpansee versus gibbon). But since I'm now working with mean shapes (to match the nodes of the phylogenetic tree to the datapoints), I can't run an ANCOVA because this would be like running a test on a sample size of 1. There is no variation, so it's not possible to run any statistical test between the species when using mean shapes only.

In the PaCA, I tried to project the individuals into the shape space. The phylogenetically aligned components are variables as any other, so it should be possible to run analysis to see how the species differ. However, there is still the issue about spurious groups ... I could try to fix this according to the paper of Thioulouse et al. 2021.

I've also read some information on a 'phylogenetic PCA', but I don't know for sure if this can be used when working with mean shapes. Other papers, for example Lewton 2015, don't use a phyPCA due to its efficacy in studies of adaptation (I also don't know how to map the individuals in the shape space here because of the transformation of the residuals), but they mapped a phylogeny onto the standard PCA to visualize the effect of phylogeny on morphology in the morphospace. Locomotor group differences in principal component scores were then investigated using pANOVA.

Could someone help me with clarifying what would be the best approach here?
Thank you for clearing this up for me.

Marie.

There could probably be a better error message (we would have to catch this and have an error message that better explains why the error occurred) but the issue is caused by the invariance you create by holding constant the effect of phylogeny (species) and then having species as a term in your model.  I could replicate your issue with the plethspecies data.  I get the same error when attempting to do what you did:

> df = geomorph.data.frame(GPA, phy = plethspecies$phy, species = factor(dimnames(plethspecies$land)[[3]]))
> procD.pgls(coords ~ log(Csize) * species, data = df, phy = phy)

Error in (function (cond)  :
  error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function 'as.matrix': subscript out of bounds

I was able to produce a result by using just the interaction:

> anova(procD.pgls(coords ~ log(Csize):species, data = df, phy = phy))

Sums of Squares calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |==================================================================================| 100%

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Generalized Least-Squares (via OLS projection)
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

                   Df       SS   MS Rsq  F   Z Pr(>F)

log(Csize):species  8 0.043302    0   1  0 NaN  0.567
Residuals           0 0.000000 -Inf   0
Total               8 0.043302

Call: procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize):species, iter = iter, seed = seed,
    RRPP = TRUE, SS.type = SS.type, effect.type = effect.type,
    int.first = int.first, Cov = Cov, data = data, print.progress = print.progress)

This elucidates the issue.  There is no residual variation if species is in the model after accounting for phylogeny in estimation of model coefficients.  The reason the first attempt did not work is that in addition to the interaction, coefficients for both log(Csize) and species would be attempted first because SS.type = “I” was inherently implied, and there simply aren’t sufficient degrees of freedom to make estimation possible.  Sure enough, if we change the SS type, we can arrive at an answer.

> anova(procD.pgls(coords ~ log(Csize):species, data = df, phy = phy, SS.type = "III"))

Sums of Squares calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |==================================================================================| 100%

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Generalized Least-Squares (via OLS projection)
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type III
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

                   Df       SS   MS Rsq  F   Z Pr(>F)

log(Csize):species  8 0.043302    0   1  0 NaN  0.567
Residuals           0 0.000000 -Inf   0
Total               8 0.043302

Call: procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize):species, iter = iter, seed = seed,
    RRPP = TRUE, SS.type = SS.type, effect.type = effect.type,
    int.first = int.first, Cov = Cov, data = data, print.progress = print.progress)

This is not a good answer and is the same answer as before), but the analysis worked.  We could maybe have a better error message — if we had the foresight when one uses type I SS and a model that asks for species means after attempting to adjust estimation based on phylogenetic relatedness using the same species in the phylogeny — to explain the analysis was arrested because the user attempted something silly, but I hope you can appreciate that anticipating all illogical analyses is challenging.

The shorter response to your email could have been, “Don’t do that.” but I hope with this demonstration it is clear why you should not do that.

Best,
Mike
